title: Signs of Poor Indoor Air Quality in Your Home
h1: How Can I Tell If the Indoor Air Quality in My Home Is Bad?
description: Headaches, stuffy noses, musty smells, dust and condensation can all point to poor indoor air quality. Learn the warning signs and what to do about each one.
quick_answer: Common signs of bad indoor air include allergy or headache symptoms that ease when you leave home, dust that returns quickly, musty or chemical smells, condensation or mold, and stale or stuffy rooms. A low-cost air quality monitor can confirm what you suspect. Better filtration, ventilation and humidity control fix most problems.
body:
What health symptoms can point to bad indoor air?

Your body is often the first clue. Pay attention if you or your family notice these at home more than anywhere else:

  • Stuffy or runny nose, sneezing or itchy eyes
  • Headaches, especially in the morning or in certain rooms
  • A dry or scratchy throat and coughing
  • Asthma or allergy flare-ups
  • Feeling tired or foggy indoors

The key pattern is that symptoms ease when you're away for a while and return when you come back. These symptoms have many causes, so talk with a doctor about health concerns. But if the home is the common thread, the air is worth a closer look.

What signs can I see or smell around the house?

  • Dust that comes back fast after cleaning, or dark streaks around supply vents
  • Musty or earthy smells, which often mean moisture and mold
  • Chemical or "new" smells from paint, furniture, flooring or cleaning products
  • Condensation on windows or water stains on ceilings and walls
  • Visible mold in bathrooms, closets, around windows or on vent grilles
  • Stale, stuffy air that never seems to clear
  • Uneven temperatures and humidity from room to room

What causes poor indoor air quality?

Most problems come from a few sources:

  • Particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander and wildfire smoke
  • Moisture that leads to mold, especially in coastal homes affected by the marine layer
  • Chemicals called VOCs that off-gas from household products and building materials
  • Combustion gases from gas stoves, furnaces and water heaters
  • Too little fresh air, since newer and remodeled homes are often sealed up tight

Your HVAC system can make any of these better or worse. A dirty filter, leaky ducts pulling in attic air, or a dirty coil can spread contaminants through the whole house.

Are some rooms more likely to have bad air?

Yes. Problems often show up in specific spots first:

  • Bedrooms with closed doors overnight can build up carbon dioxide and feel stuffy by morning
  • Bathrooms and laundry rooms collect moisture, especially if the exhaust fan is weak or vents into the attic
  • Kitchens get smoke, grease and combustion gases from cooking, particularly with a gas range and no vented hood
  • Rooms next to the garage can pick up car exhaust and fumes from stored paint, fuel and chemicals
  • Rooms at the end of long duct runs may get weak airflow and feel stale

Noticing where you feel worse or where smells collect helps narrow down the cause. Keeping a few notes for a week or two, like when symptoms show up and what was happening in the house, makes it much easier to spot a pattern.

Can I measure my indoor air quality?

Yes. Consumer air quality monitors can track fine particles (PM2.5), carbon dioxide, VOCs, temperature and humidity. They're useful for spotting patterns, like particles spiking when you cook or CO2 climbing in a closed bedroom overnight.

Every home should also have working carbon monoxide alarms near sleeping areas and on each level, especially with gas appliances or an attached garage. If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.

How do I improve bad indoor air?

  1. Upgrade and change the filter on schedule. A good pleated filter is the easiest first step.
  2. Control humidity. Run bath and kitchen fans, and consider a dehumidifier in damp coastal homes or a humidifier for very dry inland air.
  3. Ventilate when outdoor air is clean. Keep windows closed during Santa Ana winds and wildfire smoke.
  4. Reduce sources by choosing low-VOC products and storing chemicals in the garage.
  5. Clean and seal the ducts if they're dirty or leaking.
  6. Add air cleaning, such as a whole-home media filter or UV light at the coil.

Our indoor air quality team can inspect your system and recommend the fixes that fit your home. If dust is the main issue, our air duct services are a good place to start.
faqs: Can poor indoor air quality make you sick?

It can contribute to allergy symptoms, headaches, irritation and asthma flare-ups, and some pollutants carry longer-term risks. If you have ongoing symptoms, see a doctor and look at your home air as a possible factor.
What is a good indoor humidity level?
Roughly 30 to 50 percent is a comfortable range for most homes. Higher levels encourage mold and dust mites, while very low levels can dry out skin and sinuses.
Do houseplants improve indoor air quality?
Not by much at normal household levels. Plants are nice to have, but filtration, ventilation and controlling the sources of pollution do far more.
Does my HVAC system affect indoor air quality?
Yes. It moves all of the air in your home, so filters, duct condition, coil cleanliness and humidity control have a direct effect on what you breathe.
What Is a Good Indoor Air Quality Level for Your Home?

Good indoor air quality usually means fine particle levels (PM2.5) at or below about 9 micrograms per cubic meter, carbon dioxide under about 1,000 ppm, relative humidity between about 30 and 50 percent, and low levels of VOCs from cleaners and new furnishings. There isn't one official score for homes, so it helps to look at each measurement separately.
